Background
By 1700, the Tsardom of Russia still lacked access to the Baltic Sea, which it had lost in the Treaty of Stolbovo in 1617. The lack of a port in the Baltic was one of the main motivators for Russia's participation in the Great Northern War. At the start of the war, the only way for Russia to transport war materials was land transport, with the only exception being its port in the White Sea, Arkhangelsk. In Arkhangelsk, Russia regularly traded with ships from England, the Dutch Republic, and the Hanseatic cities.
of a painting of Carl Magnus Stuart by Otto Wallgren from 1849]]
Thus, preventing this was of great importance for Sweden, as it was also an opportunity to isolate Russia from the ocean. The first suggestion for a Swedish expedition to the port was first proposed by a person in Vasa, who offered to lead peasant troops through Finland to surprise the port. Charles XII gave him the necessary weapons, but the plan was scrapped in favor of one from Carl Magnus Stuart.
Stuart suggested that 1,000–1,200 men would board archipelago ships and sail through the Neva into Lake Ladoga, proceeding through the Svir River into the Onega and then disembark at Powenez, marching towards Soma in the White Sea. From there, warships from Gothenburg would rendezvous with them and transport them to Arkhangelsk. Stuart then claimed that the troops would easily conquer the port.
Nevertheless, Stuart's plan faced criticism from a few, who feared that the Russians could harass and repel the Swedes during their transit through the Svir River and from the Onega to the White Sea, particularly during the Swedish withdrawal. Consequently, the plan was scrapped.
From his winter headquarters in Laiuse Castle on 28 February 1701, Charles XII wrote to the Governor of Gothenburg and Bohuslän, Erik Carlsson Sjöblad that he had ordered the President of the National Board of Trade, Fabian Wrede, and State secretary Samuel Åkerhielm to issue a decree regarding "the investigation of some of our frigates and other ships, at their request, to be submitted to them". Accordingly, Sjöblad visited Wrede and Åkerhielm in Stockholm to agree on further measures.
They decided that the expedition, which would set off from Gothenburg, would incorporate ships from the Gothenburg squadron and two additional frigates from Karlskrona. Additionally, a galleon, a fluyt, and another smaller ship would be hired. Men from the Life Guard stationed in Gothenburg would also board the ships for the expedition. They also required experienced navigators, and since they believed they lacked these at home, they wrote to the Governor-General of Bremen-Verden, Nils Gyllenstierna. However, Sjöblad believed it would take too long, and instead sourced them in Gothenburg and hired a navigator in Stockholm.
In order to keep the expedition a secret, Sjöblad, Wrede, and Åkerhielm claimed that the ships were going to sail to England to buy clothing, gunpowder, and ammunition for the Swedish army. On 16 April, Sjöblad reported that the ships in Gothenburg were prepared and awaiting the arrival of two frigates from Karlskrona. However, their arrival was delayed. When Wrede sent Hans Wachtmeister to bring the ships from Karlskrona, Carl Henrik von Löwe, the appointed leader of the expedition, had already departed on a cruise off Danzig. A fast-sailing ship was sent after him, delaying the arrival of one frigate until 20 April. On May 9, the second frigate arrived in Gothenburg, and both were prepared after 2 days, receiving provisions and troops from the garrison before departing, only reaching New Älvsborg due to strong winds.
Expedition
Carl Henrik Löwe would lead the expedition; he designated the frigate Varberg as his flagship. Carl Hans Wachmeister would command the ship itself. In total, the Swedish fleet consisted of seven warships with 131 guns altogether. They also had 828 sailors on board. Additionally, two companies from the Life Guard, around 300 men, would also board the ships, led by Gustaf Lilliecrona and O. Boström. Lastly, artillery lieutenant Hans Gabriel Stjerna, with two mortars, 60 and 80 pounders respectively, participated.
Once the ships were out to sea, everyone onboard was ordered to report to von Löwe, who read out the king's instructions for the expedition. First, they were to prevent further trade into Arkhangelsk by the Dutch, English, and the free cities of Bremen, Hamburg, Lübeck, and Emden. The squadron was to arrest and search all merchant ships that it encountered. They would confiscate the cargo if pre-existing treaties with the aforementioned nations allowed it. Secondly, the expedition aimed to enter Arkhangelsk, setting fire to the city and the Russian ships while also plundering, destroying, and taking everything that they could. In order to motivate the troops participating, they would receive a quarter of the value of all ships captured and condemned to prize, along with half of what would be taken from Arkhangelsk.
Should the city be captured, the Swedes were to release all merchant vessels belonging to allied nations if possible. If that could not be done, they were instructed to assess the cargo's value and provide compensation. Once the city had been destroyed, they would seal off the harbor by scuttling ships in its approaches. The orders further exempted the squadron from observing customary naval courtesies toward foreign warships, allowing them to avoid identification as Swedish vessels by striking their guns below deck or sailing under foreign flags.

After handing out the instructions, the expedition continued. The squadron arrived off the western coast of Norway by 22 June, receiving fresh fish. On the following day at noon, the squadron spotted a Russian lodja anchored at Creutx Island. Lieutenant Johan Alin was ordered to man a sloop to take the lodja, being prevented from escaping by the Mjöhunden. The lodja promptly surrendered, with the Swedes taking its entire cargo. They also took the 26 men, four young boys, and two women on board as prisoners. On 25 June, the squadron passed a village where several Russian lodja's were anchored, but the Swedes did not attack to avoid the Russians finding out about the expedition. On 26 June, the Swedish fleet anchored at Modeski, hoisting English flags. Once this had been done, a Russian boat sailed towards the fleet, manned by Russian soldiers under the command of Nicolai Kikanon. The Swedish troops were sent below deck and the guns were covered as Kikanon boarded the ship.
According to Löwe, Kikanon noticed the cannons, resulting in a shift in his demeanor. Despite this, Kikanon and his translator Mikael Boris were invited into the cabin. When Löwe noticed their suspicion, he quickly imprisoned them and the 16 men onboard their boat. The translator was questioned on who gave them foreknowledge on the Swedish expedition, and it was revealed that the Dutch had told the Russians about it three weeks prior. A Swedish council of war was convened as a result, where the translator claimed that there were 54 or more foreign merchant ships in Arkhangelsk. Alexis Petrovitz Proforskoj, the governor of the city, had brought in 1,200 men in two regiments to reinforce the garrison, originally 600 men. He also began construction of a fortress in the narrowest part of the harbor, assisted by the Dutch.
